But certain aspects of the matter have arisen in debate which commend themselves to me as subjects for comment. Perhaps I would not have spoken at all had it not been for the fact that I felt some member from each province should make a statement. So far, hon. members from my province of Manitoba have not taken part in the debate, and I felt that one should.
So far as I am concerned-and I am sure in this respect I speak for many, indeed, if not all, my colleagues-I would support the motion, because in the first place I believe it is a most reasonable proposition. Hon. members have not attacked the basic idea of this redistribution resolution. I am not sure that that is the course they would have followed had they had a little more temerity. At any rate, whether or not they had the courage to do so, the fact is that they have not attacked the fairness of this sort of redistribution. It does not seem to me that it is possible to attack it. It is, after all, an attempt to seize again the principle under which we desire to operate our political life, the principle we accepted in 1867.
In 1867, without doubt, we had representation by population; but before long we failed to have it, by reason of what has been termed the "joker" clause in the British North America Act, as a result of which undoubtedly Ontario came to have a greater representation than she would have been entitled to have under a strict representation-by-population distribution.
True, even in the beginning the principle was mitigated to a certain extent by ideas of territorial representation. But on the whole it was representation by population that the fathers of confederation sought; and that is the principle to which all Canadians have subscribed from that day onward-although it would seem to me, in the light of the voting of the Progressive Conservative party to date, that sometimes that subscription was more in the nature of lip service than it was sincere.
Before dealing with what I consider some of the practical aspects of the compact theory which has been advanced, I should like to address a few remarks to the thoughts left with us by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). He has complained- and he is about the only one-about the effects of the resolution before us, because he does not think it is quite fair to British Columbia. But, Mr. Speaker, British Columbia is to be assigned that number of members which its population warrants, according to the latest authoritative count. British Columbia, like every other province, must receive according to its population, and according to some

definite count. The last authoritative count was in 1941, and we have to operate on that basis, or on some other. It is true that estimates of population can be made between then and now; but we cannot take estimates. We cannot proceed on the basis of any other sort of count than that which has always been the accredited manner of checking up on the number of our people.
As a matter of fact, British Columbia is better off when she is receiving two additional members, as a result of using the 1941 census, than she would be if we deferred the matter until 1951. That is to say, clearly she is going to suffer an injustice if we do not have this distribution; she has been suffering an injustice right along, and the present procedure will take care of that to a certain extent.
The complaint coming from the hon. member from New Westminster amuses me somewhat, bearing in mind as I must the number of times he has inveighed against the Japanese and Chinese. You know, out in British Columbia at the present time, under the 1941 census and by reason of this distribution, the hon. member for New Westminster and the people of that province will be accorded an additional member of parliament by reason of the fact that there are in their midst a large number of Japanese, Chinese and other orientals. These people cannot vote.

speechtext:
That question also is very easy to answer. However, it is not worth answering, and I will deal with it in another way. It is so involved and so unclear that it becomes silly and, therefore, should not be dealt with. Let us look at this compact theory which is being supposedly seriously-advanced to-day by the Tory party. Let us get away from all question of what is written in certain records, of what is written in the law itself and deal only with the simple proposition that three or four provinces came together and as a result of their discussions an agreement was made and a law was passed, and, therefore, the law cannot be changed. That is the principle that the Tory party would import into the domestic constitutional politics of this country. I believe I know where they get their inspiration. They have observed, as we all have observed, the veto principle which has been incorporated into the proceedings of the united nations. Every person regrets the veto arrangement, although it is understandable why it should be there. These gentlemen of Canada's Tory party now desire to import that veto principle of the united nations into the domestic politics of Canada. It is a vicious principle and would be destructive of all possibility of progress.
One realizes upon examination how ridiculous it is. There were three organizations, one called the colony of Nova Scotia, another called the colony of New Brunswick and another called the colony of Canada; to-day there are nine provinces in a nation called Canada, and it is suggested that these nine must be consulted because an agreement was
Redistribution

made. In the first place the government of Alberta made no agreement; the "agreement" was made only by Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Canada. There are only two of the makers of this supposed agreement who could be consulted at all. If you wanted to consult the three parties, whom would you consult? Would you consult the legislature which is headed by Mr. Drew', or the legislature which is headed by Mr. Duplessis? Neither one of them to-day represents the Canada of 1866. The Canada of 1866 passed out of existence. There is no continuing body that could be consulted and the practical difficulties in the way of the compact theory are insuperable in themselves.
Then take my own province. Manitoba had no hand in making the "agreement". Manitoba is in confederation by virtue of the fact that certain money was paid to a private company for the land and for the jurisdiction and for the monopolies it held over the country. That province has no right to ask for any form of consultation at all. The same is true of the two great provinces that were called the northwest territories. The territories of that time became the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. They could not make any agreement because they did not exist. They were owned, lock, stock and barrel, by the Hudson's Bay Company. The Hudson's Bay Company had jurisdiction over them as well as owning all the land. The Hudson's Bay Company passed laws for them. They certainly made no agreement about coming in, so how could they be consulted?
If it be said that these three provinces by reason of their being brought in as provinces were granted the same rights as the other provinces, I would say that is correct. But the word "rights" imports a legal enactment, imports something written down, some record that is discoverable some place. So far as the compact theory advocates in this house have shown there is certainly no law granting a right of consultation. They say there .is no law granting this right, but there ought to be. That is virtually their position. These three provinces have come in with all the rights of the other provinces, but they get only the rights that there are in law. After hearing the dissertation of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) last evening and of the hon. member who just sat down a short time ago, it would seem to be clear that there certainly are no legal rights of consultation.
I do not think any person will deny that in the years just before 1867 there was an agreement. There was an agreement between outstanding men in those various colonies. The Minister of Justice quoted from an essay by

Kennedy who said that they were men who transcended the institutions of which they were a part. Undoubtedly those men got together and made an agreement. But there is no evidence even there to suggest that they made an agreement providing for the colonies from which they came being consulted thereafter in the event of any change being desired. The true nature of the agreement they made on that particular point is made clear in a passage to be found in the life of George Brown, and another passage in the same book from the life of Sir John A. Macdonald. We will see the nature of the agreement with reference to representation by population if we take a glance at a paragraph in the life of George Brown which appears on page 83 in the Makers of Canada series. Dealing with something which the opening sentence does not adequately disclose and which does not matter at the moment for the purposes of the text, the paragraph reads:
Lower Canada complained of the injustice, and with good reason.
That was the injustice of gerrymandering, as it was called, the two parts of Canada by giving them equal representation. It goes on:
In the course of time Lord Durham's prediction was fulfilled; by immigration the population of Upper Canada overtook and passed that of Lower Canada. The census of 1852 gave Upper Canada a population of nine hundred and fifty-two thousand, and Lower Canada a population of eight hundred and ninety thousand two hundred and sixty-one. Brown began to press for representation by population. He was met by two objections. It was argued on behalf of the French Canadians that they had submitted to the injustice while they had the larger population, and that the Upper Canadians ought to follow their example. Mr. Brown admitted the force of this argument, but he met it by showing that the Lower Canadians had been underrepresented for eight years, and that by the time the new representation went into force, the Upper Canadians would have suffered injustice for about an equal term, so that a balance might be struck. A more formidable objection was raised by Mr. Hincks, who said that the union was in the nature of a compact between two nations having widely different institutions; that the basis of the compact was equal representation, and that Brown's proposition would destroy that basis. Cartier said that representation by population could not be had without repeal of the union. The French Canadians were afraid that they would be swamped, and would be obliged to accept the laws and institutions of the majority.
That was the sort of picture which these men had in front of them when they came to make an agreement and submit it to what was then called the mother parliament. And later, respecting it, Sir John A. Macdonald said:
The vexed question of representation by population was solved in a manner justly styled by Macdonald "equally ingenious and simple ' since it granted this much desired boon without joining thereto his bugbear of manhood suffrage.

"By adopting the representation of Lower Canada as a fixed standard," he said, "as the pivot on which the whole would turn-that province being the best suited for the purpose, on account of the comparatively permanent character of its population, and from its having neither the largest nor the least number of inhabitants, we have been enabled to overcome the difficulty I have mentioned. We have introduced the system of representation by population without the danger of an inconvenient increase in the number of representatives on the recurrence of each decennial period. The whole thing is worked by a simple Rule of Three. For instance, we have in Upper Canada 1,400,000 of a population; in Lower Canada, 1,100,000. Now, the proposition is simply this, if Lower Canada with its population of 1,100,000 has a right to sixty-five members, how many members should Upper Canada have, with its larger population of 1,400.000? The same rule applies to the other provinces, the proportion is always observed'and the principle of representation by population carried out. If an increase is made. Lower Canada is still to remain the pivot on which the whole calculation will turn."
Those two passages show the difficulties of those days, and Macdonald's clear statement afterwards shows that what they were agreeing upon was a principle, not a particular clause in a law such as the law we are now dealing with, which refers to a one-twentieth decrease in population before any change in the representation can be effected. They wanted to introduce the principle of representation by population, and they thought they had done it, and we found out in the course of time that they had not done it. All that it is desired to do now is to return to the condition in which the fathers of confederation thought they had left this country. There is no more to the proposal before us than that, to adhere to the general principle of representation by population, mitigated in respect to certain sections by certain constitutional changes we have already made granting a degree of territorial representation.
I will go so far as to say that I do not think there is any part of the constitution that requires consultation of provinces by this parliament before- it votes an address to the British parliament for a change in the British North America Act. There is no part of our constitution in my opinion where that would be legally necessary. I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) gave a complete answer to the argument for the need of protection of minorities in this country when he spoke last night. I would not deny and I do not think anyone would deny the wisdom of consulting the provinces when a matter may be dealt with which affects their rights particularly. I do not think any person would deny that. It would be the part of wisdom to consult them just as they were consulted a few years back when the dominion took over
by virtue of a constitutional change the power to legislate with respect to unemployment insurance. The Prime Minister at that time carried on a lengthy series of negotiations by way of consultation with the provinces, and after a satisfactory condition of assent had been received all round, he was able to recommend the appropriate resolution to result in legislation by this house. That is an example of the wisdom of proceeding in that way, against an absolute right of consultation.
Having regarded this matter from the viewpoint of the practical difficulties in the way of consultation; practical difficulties in the way of what is called the compact theory, I conclude with this. I agree entirely with what several speakers have said, particularly the speaker just before me, in reference to amending the British North America Act in Canada. I am, you know, in fiscal matters in favour of as easy an importation policy as possible, and I think we ought to signalize our belief in almost free importation by importing the British North America Act itself into this country. I think that the sooner we do that the better. I have spoken on this subject before. I think it is most outrageous and an anachronism that this parliament should have to be sending over to the old country sasnng: "Please pass this law for us." It is not merely derogatory of our own dignity but it is definitely insulting to the ideas of dignity of the parliament at Westminster. I think it is an effrontery on the part of this country to continue to use the parliament at Westminster as a chore boy. It may very well be that this debate will have the result of bringing some relief in that respect. It may very well be that this country will see that its present way of attempting constitutional change cannot be continued. I am not in a position to say at the moment what would be the right way in which this country should proceed from now on to amend its constitution. It might begin by allowing matters to develop, just as the British methods of legislation have grown over there. That is not so important at this moment. The main thing is to take on the authority and the power to amend our own constitution, and not to keep going on these constant pilgrimages to Westminster that have been necessary whenever changes in our constitution were desired.
I have always been impressed with the suggestion made by the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe. His view was that we might effect an amendment to our constitution by a two-thirds majority vote of the provinces. He thought that should be sufficient to carry an amendment of the constitution in anything except
Redistribution

racial and religious matters, but in. the case of an amendment trenching upon these two subjects there would have to be unanimity. Well, that seems to me to be a pretty reasonable way of proceeding, a fairly reasonable formula. However, I am not wedded to any particular formula, but I am very strongly in favour of the idea that Canadians had better begin to act as members of a nation, and not members of a colony as we were in 1867, and that we should do our own work hereafter, and not keep passing it over to Westminster after long debates of this sort.

Mr. Speaker, the redistribution
proposal that is now before us seems to be something in the nature of an act of munificence and generosity toward some provinces, and especially Quebec. The latter is told: you will have eight more members. However, the constitution must first be amended and for that purpose a procedure which I deem improper and irregular is being resorted to. The British North America Act is considered by the government as an ordinary legislation which can be amended at will and according to the whim of the party in power. It is now desired to amend its provisions so as to give Quebec a few more members, but at some future time it will again be amended to her detriment. That is an unfair procedure as well as a serious blow to national unity.
The provinces, which were parties to the federal covenant, are not consulted while Westminster, which has nothing to do with our affairs except to play the part of the notary who certifies a document, in the words of the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe is called upon to give its consent to the proposal. The London government is to change our constitution and the provinces will have to abide by its decision.
It is perhaps imagined that the granting of a few more members to Quebec will silence the legitimate claims of those who, in that province, believe that confederation is more than an ordinary piece of legislation out a treaty, a covenant which cannot be altered without the consent of the contracting parties. The stand taken by the province of Quebec is clear-cut and logical. If, because she found it momentarily advantageous, she agreed to the principle implied in the act which the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) has brought to our attention, the other provinces would consider her to be making a mere show of sincerity, and her behaviour would mean that she is prepared

to allow the central government to change the constitution whenever such change is to her advantage and that she will oppose a change only when it is of benefit to others.
She would be an accomplice in sabotaging the achievement of the fathers of confederation and her attitude would bear out her belief that the British North America Act is a mere bauble in the hands of the Ottawa centralists.
Confederation has been a compact between the provinces; it has been one, especially, between the two races in this country. The fathers of confederation were the first to say so.
(Text):
Speaking in the house on February 3, 1865, Sir John A. Macdonald, in introducing the resolutions adopted at the Quebec conference, referred to what he called the "treaty of union" which had taken place. Sir John further said:
The government desire to say that they presented the scheme as a whole, and would exert all the influence they could bring to bear in the way of argument to induce the house to adopt the scheme without alteration, and for the simple reason that the scheme was not one framed by the government of Canada, or by the government of Nova Scotia, but was in the nature of a treaty settled between the different colonies, each clause of which had been fully discussed and had been agreed to by a system of mutual compromise.
On February 6, in the legislative council, Hon. Alexander Campbell referred again as follows to the scheme, which was not the work of the government alone, but that of delegates of all the other provinces. "It was the result of deliberation, accommodation and compromise," he said.
On February 6, Sir John A. Macdonald further said:
As I stated in the preliminary discussion, we must consider this scheme in the light of a treaty.
I trust this scheme will be assented to as a whole. I am sure this house will not seek to alter it in its unimportant details and, if altered in any important provisions, the result must be that the whole will be set aside and we must begin de novo. If any important changes are made, every one of the colonies will feel itself absolved from the implied obligation to deal with it as a treaty. Each province will feel itself at liberty to amend it ad libitum so as to suit its own views and interests.
On February 8, Hon. George Brown, resuming the debate on the resolutions, said:
This scheme cannot be carried and no scheme can be. that has not the support of both sections of the province, . . .(Ontario and Quebec).
It was necessarily the work of concession: not one of the thirty-three framers but had, on some points, to yield his opinions.
On February 9, Hon. D'Arcy McGee went further and said:

In 1914, Viscount Haldane stated that the British North America Act-

Now let us examine some of the views expressed by Canadian statesmen and jurists. In 1883 Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated:
I repeat, each time that this parliament (Ottawa) succeeds in depriving a province of a right which it holds, no matter how insignificant such right may be, it is a step further along the path leading to legislative union.

It is an historical fact that the federal form of government was adopted solely in order that Quebec might retain the exceptional and unique position which it occupied on the American continent.

In the course of our work we have come to appreciate as never before the achievements of the fathers of confederation. In his handbook of parliamentary law, His Honour Justice Mignault, after showing that Canada is a federal union, added: "Confederation is but the fulfilment of a pact entered into by four provinces."

Reverend Father Louis Lachance, O.P., has said:
Every constitution, except in cases where the instinct of savagery must be repressed through the use of force, is necessarily a contract.
If the consent of the provinces was needed for the establishment of confederation, it follows that the constitution cannot be amended without their concurrence. May I quote for the benefit of those who claim that the constitution is just an ordinary piece of legislation, what Mr. Leo Pelland had to say in a March 1936 issue of L'Action Catholique:
What is a legislation based upon an agreement, a compromise, and retaining some of the features of such agreement and compromise, if not a legislation having a clearly contractual character ?
Mr. Maurice Ollivier has made the following statement at page 68 of his book "Problems of Canadian Sovereignty":
Those who hold that our constitution is a contract are on quite safe ground, and they can easily find, throughout our history, outstanding men who have shared their views or used the term "federal pact."
Confederation is a contract between two [DOT] races and, as was so forcibly stated by Father Richard Ares:
If there exists to-day a Canadian confederation rather than a centralized state, it is first and foremost because of the explicit will of Lower Canada.
Upper Canada preferred a legislative union.
An English-speaking Canadian, Mr. John Boyd, had this to say in his book "Sir Georges Etienne Cartier, Baronet":

Without Cartier, Quebec's assent to the union would certainly have been impossible to obtain, and without Quebec confederation would never have been more than a noble dream.
The provinces are deprived of a sacred right when the constitution is amended without any previous consultation with them.
At the present time Quebec is not willing to barter away her rights for eight, ten or event twenty seats in this house. Respecting as she does the rights of others, she wants the rights conferred to her by the constitution to be respected. speechtext:
If my hon. friend will bear with me he will find that I am not against the principle of granting eight or ten additional members to the province of Quebec; I am against the proposed method of achieving this result. Most assuredly it is the duty of the members of the dominion parliament at Ottawa to deal with federal matters, as defined by the constitution, but it is untrue to claim that they have authority to amend the constitution itself.
If the representation of the province of Quebec is to be increased, so much the better, and I am all for it; the price of this recognition of our rights should not be the destruction of the very foundation of our Canadian constitution.
I claim that the right to amend our constitution belongs jointly to the provinces and to the dominion.
The London parliament only ratifies decisions taken here. Once again I quote Mr. Lapointe on this subject:
The British North America Act, says he, is the result of lengthy and complicated deals, and finally of a compromise which the provinces approved through their officially accredited representatives. We have, therefore, a legal agreement, drawn up in due form, and freely ratified. Hence, the power to alter our national constitution is vested in the provinces whose good will made the alliance possible and whose unanimous good will is requisite to effect any desired amendment.
As for Westminster, we might say that it merely fulfilled notarial functions when the compact of 1867 was entered into and its present duties, similar to those of the past, consist in no more than authenticating the clauses of the Canadian federal agreement.
For these reasons, I shall vote in favour of the amendment.

speechtext:
The hon. member is perhaps not sufficiently aware of his responsibilities to feel sorry about it. But when he pits himself against the recognized right of fair representation in this country, he should realize that we have to feel sorry in his stead.
It had not been my intention, Mr. Speaker, to share in this discussion, for in marshalling arguments from this country's foremost constitutional and political authorities, the speeches you have heard so far made it unnecessary for me to take part in this debate. This resolution is so clearly based on justice that its discussion should have appeared unnecessary and it should have carried without comment or opposition. Until this afternoon however, the debate had remained on a plane and within bounds worthy of admiration.
The advocates and opponents of the measure have gone into the constitutional and the legal aspects of the matter, and have reviewed it from the standpoint of justice and common sense, with such skill and logic that I feel the voice of Chicoutimi should have remained silent. It is also because I am from the lower St. Lawrence region that I should not like to give the impression that . this voice, however pleasant, expresses the feelings and the thoughts of our people.
This resolution concerns not only the premier of Quebec and his followers, but every Canadian citizen. It involves constitutional law and is highly important from a national standpoint; it is in the first place a measure of fair play. I wish to pay special tribute to the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) who has dealt masterfully with this question with the calm and the competence of an eminent statesman.
This resolution is based upon law and justice. I shall not enter into legal technicalities;
I shall not attempt to recall utterances of past and present statesmen or to quote the sections of the constitution. Such quotations have been numerous during this debate. However, if we examine the quotations submitted to the house, we find that, on the whole, the authorities on parliamentary law hold that the dominion, in matters coming within its purview, is not subservient to the provinces in regard to the amendments or adjustments to be made to the constitution. It is necessary to distinguish between external sovereignty and internal sovereignty, as it were. In regard to the administration of provinces, to their own

jurisdiction, undoubtedly no Canadian government would entertain the idea of amending our constitution without consulting the provinces. But as regards powers exclusively reserved to the federal government- namely our external relations-things are different. So far as the right of the hon. member for Chicoutimi to sit in this house is concerned, it is the responsibility of his constituents. Besides, I believe the hon. member for Chicoutimi is entitled to speak for himself but not on behalf of the Hon. Mr. Duplessis. After hearing all the arguments of all those who took part in this debate and especially the speech of the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret), whom I take pleasure in commending specially, I believe we may admit as a matter of principle so that in the matter of representation, the federal government has the undoubted right of amending its constitution, in order to redress a wrong resulting from a false interpretation of this document. However, if there were any kind of doubt-and to my mind there is none-I fail to see, if there were any doubt, Mr. Speaker, should it prevent us from acting on a matter of absolute justice? Is there a single member in this house who, prior to fulfilling a duty of plain justice, would say:	I shall refrain from acting due to a
technicality, to a mere doubt and I shall adopt an attitude which will prevent the interested parties from obtaining justice. Mr. Speaker, we seem to recognize unanimously that it is a matter of plain justice. This may be gathered from the statements of the hon. members for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Chicoutimi admitted that this is the case. But, Mr. Speaker, if our province has an absolute right to a representation corresponding to its population, are we authorized to resort to excuses and technicalities in order to shirk our duty and deprive our province of eight representatives? Mr. Speaker, the resolution now before the House reflects completely the wishes of all the provinces. It provides for representation of the provinces on the basis of population while protecting minority groups in Prince Edward Island and the Yukon. This resolution favours representation according to population in all parts of the country, it is in the interest of Canada for it prevents any province from gaining undue advantage

Redistribution
to the prejudice of others. It allows all parties and all groups to express their views adequately in parliament.
The arguments set forth against the present resolution seem quite specious to me. Some say:	"The measure is fair and should be
passed, but not before the provinces are consulted. If any province objects to it, it cannot be passed. Therefore we shall vote against the resolution so that the provinces might be consulted and the measure thereby defeated." Such is the logic of the opponents of the resolution. They fight for an alleged principle founded neither on law nor justice to prevent the adoption of a fair and just measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Who sounded the alarm?
Who are the opposition?
Perhaps from a letter written by the Quebec premier. This brings to my mind the words from Holy Writ "The letter killeth but the spirit giveth life." The letter of the Quebec premier will kill him, because it is against the rights of the province of Quebec. Unfortunately, as a result we shall soon lose the company of the young member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon) who has listened to his master's voice. Hearing him a few moments ago, and looking at him, I said to myself: "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau." And that French voice from the province of Quebec has been raised in opposition to the granting of some rights to the French element in Canada and in the province of Quebec. That is why I have deemed it my duty, on behalf of the French-speaking group, who were the first to come to this country and whom we represent in this house, in the name of those among the fathers of confederation who were Frenchspeaking, and who wanted to include in the constitution the means whereby we could obtain a fair and proportionate representation, on their behalf, Mr. Speaker, I have deemed it my duty to protest against such a treasonable act.
Some people hide behind a screen, they put on a mask, and they use the bugbear of autonomy in order to avoid facing the true situation and doing their duty. Will the autonomy of the province be better upheld if there are eight less or eight more members? Does not the value of Quebec's autonomy lie in the worth of her
sons, in the endeavours of her representatives in a fair and equitable representation in this house? Does not our duty to the autonomy of the province consist in following the example of the fathers of confederation and endeavouring to protect the spirit rather than the letter of the constitution, which latter course would entail the risk of distorting it, especially in so far as the province of Quebec is concerned? The autonomy of the province of Quebec lies solely in her right of administration, of government, of management, within the exclusive limits of her jurisdiction, especially in matters of education, language and religion.
Should sections 92 and 93 and even section 133 of the British North America Act be amended without consulting the provinces. I am sure that the honourable members both on this side of the house and opposite would rise in protest against such action; they would want to prevent the spoliation of our rights and the sabotaging of the constitution, and, finally, to ward off civil war in this country. To-day we are dealing with a right which must be granted to all citizens of Canada, of whatever race, creed or language.
Mr. Speaker, as I said at the outset, I am scandalized to find that an honourable member, heeding his master's voice, should have risen in this Canadian parliament in order to prevent French Canadian influence from becoming greater and stronger in this house.
Mr. Speaker, we have been elected by people of our language, our creed and our race.
These citizens have shown their faith in us; they have given us a mandate, for what purpose? For the purpose of representing them here and safeguarding their rights. It is our right to have a representation proportionate to our population, and it is our duty to demand that right-I regret, however, that the hon. member for Chicoutimi had to leave the house before he was convinced-it is our duty to claim that right and we shall be united in trying to obtain proportionate representation for our province and also for the other provinces, according to their population.
When the question of representation in the Canadian parliament arises, when administration and internal economy or external affairs of Canada are concerned, do we, who have been elected to the national parliament, to

represent our electors and the whole of Canada, and to legislate for and safeguard the future of our country, do we have to consult Mr. Duplessis who, for political purposes, will say that we want to sabotage the British North America Act? I feel sorry for the hon. member for Chicoutimi, who will have to answer not only to his constituency but to his province and to future generations for the step he has taken to-day. He will be responsible for the gesture which, translated into words, means that the children who are called upon to replace us will have no say in the nation's business because his leader in Quebec was not consulted, and that the hon. member does not wish them to have a fair representation in the Canadian parliament.
This may be the voice crying in the wilderness, but it is not the voice of John the Baptist, patron saint of French Canadians, since the voice of John the Baptist brought prosperity and happiness to people of good will. This other voice, however, sows the seeds of sadness and death. Under the present system, Mr. Speaker, even though the population of Quebec increased to five millions while that of Ontario would be at the four million level, the latter province would still have seventeen more representatives than the former. If the provinces are consulted, one alone need dissent to deprive us from Quebec or you from British Columbia or any of the others from representation in proportion to its population.
The hon. member for Outrermont has explicitly defined the issue from this viewpoint. Some hon. members opposite, realizing that consultation with their provincial colleagues from Ontario would defeat t'he measure, object to it on the grounds that such advice is not sought.
It gave me great pleasure to hear the sympathetic hon. member for Eglinton, but it will require more than the French section of his speech, which was very well delivered, to do justice to Quebec, as the latter is well aware. The Quebec premier simply asks that the provinces be consulted so that our lot may be settled by the premier of Ontario. If the premier of Quebec is of the opinion that the British North America Act is a treaty or a pact and that we should consult him to gain an undisputed right to eight more members, we believe that such consultation might prove dangerous and prevent t'he province of Quebec

from securing materialization of this prerogative. But let the premier of Quebec immediately declare himself willing to amend the constitution! Thus he will not give up the right to consultation which he claims as his own nor will he prevent the province of Quebec from securing adequate representation.
The hon. member for Chicoutimi said, a few moments ago, that the province of Quebec may, at some future date, be a victim to some amendment to the constitution, although it would benefit by the change now contemplated. I wonder whether the hon. member fears that a tornado will strike the province of Quebec with such force as to decimate its population or that some other cataclysm will prevent us from maintaining our proper proportion of the total population of Canada. What is certain, however, is that the population of Quebec cannot fall to the extent of determining such a spread between the relative populations of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, for at least two hundred years. Mr. Speaker, how could this amendment be even remotely detrimental to the province of Quebec? Its sole purpose is that of placing representation on a population basis. Quebec will never complain as long as it is given representation according to its population. I feel also that the other provinces will have no grounds for complaint if they have representation based on their respective populations. I have heard with my own ears a preposterous statement by a Progressive Conservative member for Prince Edward Island, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure), who complains about this measure, although, under its provisions, his province would be granted four representatives. This hon. member was opposed to the principle of representation based on population. Nevertheless, this measure takes care to safeguard the minorities of Prince Edward Island and Yukon.
May I say here that the hon. member for Chicoutimi has spoken of centralization by the Ottawa government? The fact is that we are endeavouring to decentralize, giving to Quebec the number of members to which she is entitled. We want thereby to have more members from Quebec to take part in the management of the country.
He tells us that to-day we are being generous to the province of Quebec. We are

R edistribution
not being generous, we are not rewarding Quebec. We are granting it exactly what we are giving the other provinces, nothing else. He said that the	province of
Quebec was not to be bought with eight or twenty seats.	Does the hon. member
wish to imply that we, the representatives of the province of Quebec, have been paid to obtain these additional seats? And what of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion), who sits next to the hon. member for Chicoutimi, has he been paid to support the resolution under consideration?
In conclusion he said: why not abolish the provincial legislature if it has been decided, in order more securely to entrench dictatorship in Ottawa, not to consult the provinces? Well, Mr. Speaker, dictatorship, in Ottawa, is in the hands of 245 hon. members who constitute parliament; in the next house, dictatorship will be exercised by the 255 members who will have been elected to sit here. Is representation of the people by the men of their choice to be called dictatorship? However, these members must speak for themselves and their constituents and not on behalf of members from other legislatures. As for me, I speak as member for Kamouraska. The hon. member from Chicoutimi does not speak for the electors of his constituency but on behalf of the prime minister of the province of Quebec. However, that is his own business.
We have a specific mandate and special responsibilities. We have a duty to perform here and we do have to take into account any instructions given by provincial members. As a federal Liberal member, I do not have to take orders from any provincial legislature although I am always open to suggestions and advice. But, Mr. Speaker, when members of a provincial legislature attempt to invade the field of federal legislation, I think we should be sufficiently proud and dignified, we should have, to a sufficient degree, the courage of our own convictions to defend the rights of our race and our province and to ensure their triumph.
In closing, I wish to state definitely that I shall never hide behind a screen, that I shall never seek cover behind a curtain and that I shall never shirk my responsibilities.
We now have before us a measure of the utmost importance designed to establish a representation according to population, that will be fair to all provinces. In considering this measure, mindful of my country's future, mindful of the voters of my constituency, and of my family, I feel it my duty to support this resolution as a Canadian imbued with truly national feelings.
Mr. GEORGES H. HEON (Argenteuil) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, after the grandiloquent speech of the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Marquis), I was almost reluctant to address the house. However, every hon. member has a part to play under his oath of office, in accordance with the interests of his constituents. I would like as a French Canadian from the province of Quebec, to express myself briefly in French as follows on the matter now before the house.
Had it not been amply established by parliamentary debates in the last fifty years, had not that fact been brutally disclosed by several interprovincial conferences, had it not been emphasized by numerous decisions in our courts of justice, the present debate on the redistribution bill (which does away with the principle of a pivotal province which had caused so much worry to Cartier) would show luminously on what weak foundations our federal structure is built, how difficult it is to govern a country where ten sovereign parliaments are to be found in fields which have been more or less clearly allocated to them; where are to be found also racial groups of different origins and mentalities, languages and religions, with different economic problems and political creeds which cover all the ground from repulsive communism to complete centralizing socialism and even to miserly and extreme capitalism, from a broad and sincere Canadianism to an avowed imperialism, which is sometimes concealed under a more or less hypocritical internationalism, depending on whichever attitude is necessary to insure an immediate political triumph.
The numerous and excellent speches made to date on the measure now before us and which I have read with care, show conclusively the inevitable clash of these various trends of opinion. Personally-and I wish to emphasize this fact-I do not question the sincerity of all members of this house, convinced as I am that they are all eager to serve their country and their constituents well.
We must accordingly respect such divergent opinions, inasmuch as they represent the beliefs of important groups (at least, of groups which think they are important) in our country. In such a matter, it would be wise to follow the advice given by scholarly Father Simard, on page 144 of his book entitled: "Pour L'education dans un Canada souverain," which I beg to quote:
Redistribution

That fact must be taken into account in our parliamentary era. Because politics, to be effective, must enlist the cooperation of the people it follows that discussion of public questions is generalized. But weighing programs and estimating the value of social legislation are operations to be performed without injuring the respect and love which must be bestowed on men in authority, men who, in that capacity, have a right to be treated according to patriotic devotion. In that respect, our world is the saddest thing to be seen. Not only are bills and party platforms put to shreds-which is permissible- but too often are insults thrown at those who are entitled to "cult and service" as Cicero and Saint Thomas Aquinas said.

speechtext:
It is therefore in this light, Mr. Speaker, that I would like to deal very briefly with the problem before this house. We are asked to ratify a measure involving two great and divergent principles. The first one, by establishing representation on the basis of population, would grant, at this time, eight new members to the province of Quebec. Although the cry of "rep by pop" was first raised in this country by someone who feared French-Canadian preponderance, and although this principle may again operate against us, we cannot deny the immediate advantage of the proposal.
Our province and our compatriots will never have too many representatives in this house, f we consider particularly the veiled, but jonstant and crafty hostility nursed against us by certain fanatical elements, _ which is apparent not only in the civil service and the various federal departments, but in the committees and boards and sometimes even in this house.
These eight new members coming from Quebec after the next federal election, if the resolution is passed, might well mediate on this thought expressed by the same Father Simard, whom I quoted a moment ago, on page 155 of his book:
Were you to ask me now what should be said and done in parliament, I would tell you: Come to Ottawa, please, not as foreigners or as children expecting a spanking. Be thoroughly versed in questions bearing on the common good of Canada. Hold to a uniform national creed and always place it above party slogans. In this respect, all vour forefathers have sinned, the Liberals in 1905 and the Conservatives in 1912. Make it understood that Canada is both French and English and that as far as you members of the French-Canadian group are concerned, you will never divide on the three following points: freedom for our faith, freedom for our culture, a happy relation between the central and provincial authorities.
I quote further:
You may discuss the means of implementing this threefold plan. In fact, you will cling to these things above all. Not by threatening to leave your house when your rival claims it for
[Mr. Heon.i
himself, but by establishing your rights of ownership and shouting back: "You shall not oust me from my home. If you want a fight, you will have it."
The second principle involved in the resolution bears on the procedure concerning amendments to the British North America Act which may be suggested from time to time.

speechtext: I beg my 'hon. friend's pardon for interrupting him. I had not grasped what he meant.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
My hon. friend has a right to enlighten himself. I hope that I will be allowed to express forthwith my stand on this highly contentious matter, upon which even the most prominent jurists of England and of Canada are not in, agreement. In the first place, I find it absolutely ridiculous that a country such as ours should be forced humbly to pray an imperial and foreign parliament, which knows nothing or practically nothing of our political problems, to allow us to amend our own constitution. It is the weakest and the most inexcusable denial of an autonomy which exists in fact and which only an obsolete and uncalled for sentimentalism, or a dishonest concern for an immediate political advantage, prevent from freely expressing itself.
When shall we have the gumption to express our sovereignty and our autonomy by courageous and practical actions? When shall we cease to close our eyes upon the facts? Have not those tens of thousands of Canadians who made the supreme sacrifice during two world wars, in defence of freedom and of independence for the peoples of the world, gained for Canada the right to speak for herself?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friends on the government side for approving my statement. We should have the courage of our convic-

Redistribution
tions; we should take advantage of this opportunity to request the imperial parliament to waive its prerogative to approve the amendments to our constitution and to surrender to us the full and exclusive right in the matter. Let us be logical. If Canada is a free and self-governing nation, we must remove the purely artificial impediments to our freedom and autonomy.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, we should face the facts; it would be much easier for our Frenchspeaking compatriots, in view of their mentality, to give their approval to an amendment to the British North America Act, emanating from the House of Commons of Canada and her provincial legislatures, where they have their own representatives, rather than from an imperial parliament where they have no representatives. I have said so on numerous occasions and. I shall repeat it again: we should not have to ask anyone's permission; we are our own masters and the sooner we assert ourselves, the sooner we shall establish in law a situation which exists in fact and which the other nations, especially those to whom we tender a helping hand, are eager to recognize, even if only to flatter our national pride and because they are desperately in need of our assistance. Everything depends, in this respect, upon our own will, since we hold the upper hand, but our claims must be submitted with intelligence, courtesy and honesty.
Therefore the house must once more request a government which is not ours to amend our constitution. Some hon. members have referred to the procedure to be followed; several have reversed the stand which they had taken in 1943. Thus we have seen certain people who, in 1943, were in favour of amending the constitution without consulting the provinces, wdthout securing their consent, and who now claim that the consent of the provinces should first be obtained.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Who are they?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will see me after I have concluded my remarks I shall give him this information freely. Others who, in 1943, claimed! that the consent of the provinces was required, no longer voice such views this year. It is therefore a problem which everyone must solve according to his own conscience and convictions. Invectives and reproaches which may be east at one another for purely political reasons and to vent one's spleen against the premier of the province of Quebec, will not help to solve it. I am one of those who believe that we must respect, without necessarily endorsing the political convictions of the provincial and party leaders.
Coming as I do from Quebec, I have made an earnest effort in the last two weeks to ascertain the views of my constituents in respect of the proposed measure, and they appear to be as follows:
It is true that Quebec would have eight more members; however, if the constitution is thus tampered with, what guarantee have we that eventually we shall not be the losers? And if we do not protest against the method of amending our magna charta, even though such an amendment would result in an immediate and apparent advantage, how shall we later on sincerely andi seriously protest against a proposed amendment which would be detrimental to our interests?
This is then a matter of the utmost importance, which deserves the most careful consideration before a definite and final stand is taken. Personally, therefore-and I now express my own convictions, as I consulted no one and need not consult anybody-I endorse the opinion expressed by Lord Watson, Lord Haldane and Lord Sankey in the aeronautics case, by Lord Atkin in the minimum wage case, by Professor Barriedale Keith, and especially by the writer I now wish to quote. In 1939, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation asked professors of constitutional law in our Canadian universities to express over the air their legal opinion of the changes that should be made to the constitution. In the course of these talks, the province of New Brunswick was called upon to express its views, and this was done by Mr. Alfred G. Bailey, professor of British North American history at the university of New Brunswick. He was asked, at the same time-and this is important-to voice the official opinion of the New Brunswick government of which, I understand, the Hon. Mr. Dysart was then leader.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: That's right; hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I shall merely quote excerpts, for I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the house.
(Text):
The nature of the constitution, as one based on the principles of compact and consent, was formally recognized by the parliament of Canada in 1907. The Subsidy Act of that year, by which the allowances to the provinces provided in the British North America Act were to be substantially increased, was based upon the principle of consultation with the provinces. In confirmation of this principle it was acknowledged that the act of 1867 gave effect to a treaty, and that no amendment to disturb the terms of that treaty could be effected without the consent of the parties that were bound by it. The most recent recognition of the compact principle was that given by the lords of the judicial committee of the privy council, in
Redistribution

rendering judgment on certain legislation of the parliament of Canada, on January 28th, 1937. In this judgment reference was made to "the interprovincial compact to which tile British North America Act gives effect".
Moreover, it is not irrelevant to recall that the Statute of Westminster, which gave legal effept to the national status of the dominions did not increase the legislative field of the parliament of Canada at the expense of the provinces, nor did it apply to the repeal, amendment or alteration of the British North America Act, 1867 to 1930, or any order, rule or regulation made thereunder.
(Translation):
And it concludes as follows:
(Text):
In addition, it is regarded as noteworthy that the compact principle of confederation has been generally recognized in connection with the rights of racial minorities within the dominion. Few persons, perhaps no one, would have had the temerity to suggest that an amendment to the constitution which would affect the rights of a racial minority should be carried through without the consent of that minority. On the basis of the facts that have been presented it is maintained here in New Brunswick, that Canada is a confederation as prpposed at the London conference, not a federation as proposed at Quebec. This status, it is held, determines the fact that the union is based on a compact, the terms of which cannot be amended without the consent of the contracting parties; or in other words, that Canada derives its being an authority from the provinces with imperial sanction, and that this authority is a matter of agreement between the provinces. Finally, it is deemed (by the government of New Brunswick) of vital interest to demand a strict adherence to the letter and spirit of the constitution as thus conceived.
(Translation):
That is not an opinion from the province of Quebec and it is not Mr. Duplessis who speaks. Here is the opinion of an Englishspeaking province which cannot be accused of political motives and which apparently thinks along the same line as some of our Quebec fellow citizens.
Other opinions which I shall not quote may be added to that of Professor Bailey, but if we read the speeches of Hon. Honore Mercier, Sir Lomer Gouin, Hon. Alexandre Taschereau, and Hon. Maurice Duplessis, the present prime minister of the province of Quebec, we find that our constitution is a contract which may not be changed without the consent of the signatories.

Thank you, sir. By referring
indeed to the principles I set out in the 1938 by-election in Argenteuil, to the speeches I made at the Conservative party convention in Ottawa in 1938, in Winnipeg before the board of trade, in Toronto on two occasions, in Montreal at the Monument National, at Victoriaville, at Carillon and on two occasions in this house in 1939, it will be seen that my views have remained unchanged. Not later than last year, during the last election, I upheld this proposition before the electors. There is logic, therefore, in my attitude toward the measure now before us, and I am not revising my opinions. Let my constituents be my judges.
The stand taken by the province of Quebec, through its present government, on the procedure for amending our constitution is also mine, and I have no hesitation in joining them on this point; I believe that in amending our constitution, we would be creating an extremely dangerous precedent, for the following reasons. And by the way, I wish to point this out to my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Lalonde), who is listening to me.

speechtext:
I am listening very
carefully.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I am not one of those who
think that the province of Quebec should entrench itself within the walls of an absolute irredentism and be adamant on questions of details as on questions of legal principles.
Is it not true that we could better show the present situation in its proper perspective by reviewing the bargainings which preceded confederation? It can not be said that Quebec is a province like the others and has no more rights than those which were granted

R edits tribution
to the other provinces of Canada. At the time of confederation, Quebec was dealing as an equal with the other provinces and was representing a nationality more than a territorial entity. It was a compromise between two races rather than an exclusively legislative arrangement. To-day our compatriots seem to persist in this reasoning which might be expressed in the following words: You want to amend the constitution in a way that might or might not be advantageous to us, but the precedent you are creating will mean that there is no limitation in the constitution, and that you could always amend it without our assent.
We. are concerned and worried about the rights that have been conferred on us and for which Cartier had to fight unceasingly; as long as no *written guarantee excluding any possibility of amendment is given us that our rights shall forever be safeguarded as regards religion, language, customs and culture, and administration based on our financial, economic and cultural requirements as a race, we shall have to resist any proposed amendment to our constitution, because once we are headed along that path no one can tell when we shall stop. Could we not make the following suggestion: Consult us officially or otherwise, but consult us; you will obtain our approval upon whatever course is likely to help this country, but consult us, because we are one of the parties to the pact; we signed it honestly and generously. Be as honest and generous in requesting our consent to the amendments you are seeking.
To my mind, no political matter is involved in the proposition now before us and I dismiss the political angle altogether; it is rather a recurrence of the old problem of the right which the provinces who were parties to the pact have to concur in the constitutional amendment which is proposed.
There may be an immediate political advantage in the measure now contemplated, and this advantage will remain, provided our birth rate is maintained and provided we are not at some future time overwhelmed by a tide of immigration into our midst. However, should we countenance the precedent alas already established, that the British North America Act may be amended without the consent of the contracting parties, who knows but that some day a hostile group or government will not avail itself of the precedents which we have established, and change the compact to our detriment?
For, after all, there is no provision in the . British North America Act to protect us against this movement of hostility. The act makes no difference between purely administrative matters and others that we consider essential to our free development. Therefore let us at once take a definite stand. Let us say to our English-speaking fellow-citizens:	Give us the solemn and written
assurance that you will not prevent the expansion of French-speaking Canadians throughout the countiy; steep yourselves in the spirit which guided the fathers of confederation, and all will be well. You wish us to preserve national unity? We are ready and willing to do so; but please respect the spirit of the confederation compact. We are your loyal partners, but never forget that a partnership cannot endure or prosper unless its members preserve harmony and frankly and openly cooperate in the success of the undertaking. In conclusion, may I point out that last night in this house, the right hon. Minister of Justice, after admitting that from the legal point of view, section 133 of the British North America Act, bearing on the rights of the French language, could be settled-"dealt with" is used in the English text-without the consent of the provincial legislatures, spoke most eloquently of the intrinsic guarantees of human conscience. If we could forever be assured that the conscience of humanity would always remain as fair as that of the hon. members of this house, if we could, without fear, take it for granted that this same human conscience would always be guided by the uprightness and integrity which are the characteristics of our present leaders and particularly of the right hon. Minister of Justice, we might feel entirely secure in depending on it.
Unfortunately, the annals of history afford us too little assurance in that respect and record too many capricious and sudden changes of front in this same human conscience. To its eternal shame, the conscience of humanity, too often stirred up by agitators devoid of all sense of remorse or honour, opened the lengthy history of Christianity by crucifying Christ, martyrizing its apostles and disciples, and burning Joan of Arc at the stake; in modern times, it has begotten two world wars and may be sowing the seeds of a third.
Ask Poland, the small Balkan states, the masses of India and China, and the famished populations of Europe what they think of the conscience of humanity. And in our own country, what did it achieve under the guidance of certain leaders? It tolerated the hanging of the leaders of the rebellion of 1837 at Pied-du-Courant, in Montreal; it saw the exile of our present prime minister's grandfather who wanted to establish responsible government; it witnessed the hanging of Louis
Redistribution

Riel; the shameful trial of Honore Mercier, the violation of the spirit of confederation in the settlement of the school question in Manitoba, the infamous rule 17 of Ontario school laws, the acts of the Anderson government in Saskatchewan and the staccato of machine guns in the streets of Quebec in 1917.
Considering all these facts, and speaking strictly for myself under my responsibility as a private member, and because I belong to the French-Canadian minority, I prefer the security and the guarantee of a statute held as sacred, to the goodwill of the future generations who will come after us in this house and to the human conscience which might inspire their acts.
There is an amendment before the house, and I do not have to look for its motives; it calls for previous consultation with the provinces; it represents my opinion on this point, and I will support it.

In the few minutes remaining before six o'clock I should like to refer briefly to the remarks made on redistribution by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on Thursday, June 13, at page 2473 of Hansard. In this speech the minister replied to certain statements made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) and dealt at some length with conditions in the maritime provinces. In many respects his statements about the maritimes were correct, and I know the minister had no intention of being derogatory. The spirit of his remarks was constructive, and, knowing him as I do, I am certain that what he said about the maritimes was meant to be in a friendly and helpful vein. However, he made several statements which gave rise to the impression that the maritimes do not stand on their own feet. The unfortunate thing is that some local maritime papers chose to interpret these remarks as being derogatory. In an editorial, dated June 17, 1946, the Halifax Herald dealt with the minister's remarks and emphasized the fact that he accused the maritime provinces of lacking vision and initiative. It classifies the minister's statement with those made a few years ago by the minister's predecessor from Saskatchewan who said:
The chief ambitions of the maritime people were birth, marriage, death and a free ride on the intercolonial railway.

Mr. Dunning. Most emphatically I do not wish to adopt a provincial stand on behalf of the maritime provinces. I for one have always deplored that attitude and have said so in this house. Neither is it the feeling of the majority of people in the

maritimes, that they want to be provincial. They are Canadians and they want to be regarded as Canadians in every sense of the word. On the other hand, they want equally to enjoy all the benefits of Canadian citizenship on the same basis as Canadians eleswhere in Canada.
I think this house will agree history shows that maritimers, man for man, have been able to stand on their own feet in Canada or in any other country on the same basis as their fellow-Canadians. While I do not deny that vision and initiative are required wherever success is to be achieved, our problems do not all lend themselves to solution by this simple formula.
At page 2478 of Hansard the minister said that if we in the maritimes had the kind of vision as to what this country can become, we can have plants running twelve months a year. In the field of manufacturing I have known of many instances where we have been able to compete on even terms or better with our central Canadian competitors in the production of commodities.
